Liam is 33 years old. His whole family loves soccer. They love to play and watch football. He is 6 feet tall and weighs 250 pounds. He played football in college but now that he has a job at a law firm working many hours, he plays once in a while on Saturdays. His family loves to eat potatoes and meat and they often barbecue ribs and hungers that are often washed down with several beers. During week days, he normally gets coffee and doughnuts delivered to his office for breakfast and goes to lunch with clients at various restaurants. Liam knows that he has been gaining weight but stills feels pretty good. A few years ago, his cousin was diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Recently Liam’s father was diagnosed with colorectal cancer too. He now routinely visits his nutritionist for dietary advice and nutrition assessment as advised by the family doctor.

stem: Mr. John Doe is a 45-year-old male client who works as an office administrator. He is seeking nutritional advice to manage his weight. He currently stands at a height of 1.80 meters and weighs 95 kilograms. His 24-hour food recall indicates his average daily caloric intake is 2,800 kcal, and his protein intake is 90 grams. He performs light exercise 3-4 times per week (Activity Factor = 1.4). For a healthy, non-athlete adult, the standard RDA for protein is typically 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. PART A. Body Composition and Energy Requirement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Mr. Doe's Body Mass Index (BMI) and State his corresponding weight category (e.g., normal, overweight, obese).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Mr. Doe's Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) in kilocalories per day (kcal/day).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate Mr. Doe's Total Energy Expenditure (TEE) in kilocalories per day (kcal/day).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Based on his TEE and reported intake, Calculate and State his Energy Balance (in kcal/day). Part B: Protein Requirement and Analysis

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Mr. Doe's Recommended Daily Protein Requirement (RDA) in grams per day (g/day).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of his total caloric intake that is currently supplied by his reported protein intake of 90 grams.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Analyze Mr. Doe's current nutritional status by discussing his energy balance (from Part A, Qd) and his protein intake (from Part B, Qa & Qb).

parts.label: d
parts.text: What adjustment (gain/loss/maintenance) would you recommend for his weight, and why?

stem: Give four reasons for fair dismissal from an employment contract. - - Gross misconduct - - Incapacity due to ill health - - Redundancy or retrenchment - - Breach of contract terms by employee SECTION B Question 11 Japheth is a licensed dietitian running a private nutrition consultancy in Nairobi. He offers personalized dietary plans, home visits, and corporate wellness programs. Concerned about possible legal claims from clients with allergic reactions, Japheth took out a professional liability insurance policy with a local insurer. Three months later, a client filed a claim, alleging that a recommended supplement caused severe side effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two classes of insurance relevant to Japheth’s case. - Professional indemnity insurance – covers claims arising from professional advice or services. - Public liability insurance – covers claims by third parties for bodily injury or property damage on the business premises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mention six steps in the claims procedure that Japheth should follow. - - Notify the insurer promptly of the claim. - - Complete and submit the official claim form. - - Provide detailed client medical records and incident report. - - Cooperate with the insurer’s investigation. - - Attend any required mediation or dispute‐resolution meetings. - - Accept the insurer’s settlement or decide to pursue legal action.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two principles of insurance demonstrated in this case. - Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) – both parties must disclose all material facts. - Indemnity – insurance restores the insured to the financial position before the loss.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain three importance of insurance for professionals in food and nutrition. - - Risk transfer – shifts financial liability for professional claims to the insurer. - - Legal compliance – meets regulatory or contractual requirements for practice. - - Business continuity – protects against large payouts that could threaten business viability. Question 12 NutriLife Wellness Centre is a private nutrition clinic that recently dismissed Kadzo, one of its employees. The company claims that Kadzo has gross misconduct and repeated absenteeism without proper cause. However, Kadzo claims she was never issued any prior warning or disciplinary notice, as required by her employment contract. She also argues that the termination was sudden and did not follow due process as per the employment agreement she signed. She has decided to sue NutriLife for unlawful dismissal and breach of contract.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss five essential elements of a valid employment contract. - - Offer and acceptance – clear terms offered by employer and accepted by employee. - - Consideration – mutual exchange of value, e.g., salary for services. - - Capacity – parties must have legal ability to enter contract. - - Legality of object – contract’s purpose must be lawful. - - Intention to create legal relations – parties intend legal enforceability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain five possible remedies available to Kadzo following breach of her employment contract. - - Reinstatement – return to former position. - - Compensation – payment for lost wages. - - Damages – financial award for losses from breach. - - Specific performance – court order to fulfill contractual duties. - - Injunction – prevent employer from further breach. Question 13 Samantha is a registered nutritionist who has worked in a government hospital for three years. She now wants to open her own nutrition clinic and offer private dietetics services. She is unsure of the legal requirements for obtaining a private practice license from the Kenya Nutritionists and Dieticians Institute (KNDI).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify five legal and professional requirements for obtaining a KNDI private practice license. - - Valid KNDI professional registration. - - Degree or diploma in Nutrition and Dietetics from a recognized institution. - - Professional indemnity insurance coverage. - - Clean criminal record/certificate of good conduct. - - Evidence of continuing professional development (CPD) credits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline seven steps of applying for a private practice license through the KNDI portal. - - Register an account on the KNDI portal. - - Complete the online application form. - - Upload certified copies of qualifications. - - Pay the application/licensing fee. - - Schedule and pass premises inspection if required. - - Submit proof of professional indemnity insurance. - - Download and print the license upon approval.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain four consequences of practicing without a valid KNDI private practice license. - - Fines and penalties as per Nutritionists and Dietitians Act. - - Closure of the unlicensed practice. - - Professional misconduct proceedings and deregistration. - - Loss of credibility and public trust. Question 14 Food safety and hygiene are essential in preventing foodborne illnesses, particularly in informal urban food establishments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain five responsibilities of public health officers in enforcing food safety regulations under the Public Health Act. - - Inspect food premises for hygiene and compliance. - - Issue improvement notices or closure orders for violations. - - Collect and analyze food/water samples for contaminants. - - Provide education and guidance to food handlers. - - Prosecute operators for public health offenses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain five ways in which the Foods and Drugs Act helps to protect the health of consumers. - - Regulates food additives and preservatives. - - Sets labeling and packaging standards. - - Controls import/export quality of foods and drugs. - - Prohibits sale of adulterated or contaminated products. - - Enables recall of unsafe products and penalties for violations.

stem: Define the following terms:

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complex Emergency A complex emergency is a multifaceted humanitarian crisis that typically involves a combination of conflict, displacement, food insecurity, and the breakdown of essential services, often requiring international intervention.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) GAM is a measure of acute malnutrition in a population, typically defined as the percentage of children aged 6-59 months with a weight-for-height Z-score below -2 standard deviations from the median of the WHO growth standards and/or presence of bilateral edema.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Blanket Supplementary Feeding Blanket supplementary feeding is a nutrition intervention that provides additional food rations to all at-risk groups (such as children under five and pregnant/lactating women) in a given population, regardless of individual nutritional status, to prevent malnutrition.

stem: Outline four roles of the military in response to emergencies. - Providing logistical support, including transportation of food and medical supplies. - Assisting in search and rescue operations. - Setting up temporary shelters and medical camps. - Maintaining security and order in affected areas.

Highlight four objectives of Nutrition Surveillance in emergencies. - To monitor the nutritional status of the affected population. - To detect early signs of malnutrition and food insecurity. - To assess the effectiveness of ongoing nutrition interventions. - To provide data for decision-making and resource allocation.

Give five factors that lead to programme failure. - Poor planning and lack of coordination. - Inadequate funding and resource allocation. - Lack of community involvement and acceptance. - Poor monitoring and evaluation. - Insecurity and political instability.

Differentiate between rapid assessment and nutrition survey. - Rapid Assessment: A quick evaluation conducted in the early stages of an emergency to assess immediate nutrition needs and guide urgent interventions. - Nutrition Survey: A more detailed and structured data collection process used to determine the prevalence of malnutrition and inform long-term planning.

Identify five key health information assessed during nutrition emergencies. - Prevalence of acute malnutrition. - Disease outbreaks (e.g., diarrhea, measles). - Infant and young child feeding practices. - Access to clean water and sanitation. - Mortality rates (Crude Mortality Rate and Under-five Mortality Rate).

List three disadvantages of food for work nutrition intervention programme. - May exclude the most vulnerable who cannot work (elderly, disabled, pregnant women). - Can lead to exploitation and unfair labor practices. - Difficult to implement in conflict or disaster-prone areas.

State five reasons for monitoring food and nutrition responses during emergencies. - To assess the impact and effectiveness of interventions. - To ensure timely response to emerging nutritional crises. - To track resource utilization and prevent misuse. - To identify gaps and areas for improvement. - To provide evidence for policy and funding decisions.
Name five common micronutrient deficiencies during emergency. - Vitamin A deficiency. - Iron deficiency anemia. - Iodine deficiency disorders. - Zinc deficiency. - Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy).

Using the UNICEF conceptual framework, explain the causes of malnutrition. - The UNICEF conceptual framework categorizes the causes of malnutrition into three levels: immediate, underlying, and basic causes. - Immediate Causes: Inadequate dietary intake and disease. - Underlying Causes: Food insecurity, inadequate care for mothers/children, and poor health environment. - Basic Causes: Socioeconomic conditions, political instability, and lack of education. - A diagram should illustrate these connections clearly.
Nutrition intervention programmes involve different feeding strategies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain five factors for a successful General Food Distribution (GFD) programme. - Accurate population targeting and registration. - Adequate and culturally acceptable food rations. - Efficient logistics and distribution mechanisms. - Strong monitoring and accountability systems. - Coordination with other stakeholders (NGOs, government, donors).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways in which Supplementary foods are distributed. - Targeted Supplementary Feeding: Provides food to malnourished individuals based on screening criteria. - Blanket Supplementary Feeding: Provides food to all vulnerable individuals, regardless of nutritional status, to prevent malnutrition.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two criteria for admission to a selective feeding programme. - Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM): Children with weight-for-height Z-score < -3 SD or bilateral pitting edema. - Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM): Children with weight-for-height Z-score between -2 and -3 SD.

stem: Manifestation of emergencies occurs in several phases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the six phases of an emergency. - Early warning phase: Initial signs of crisis detected. - Acute emergency phase: High mortality and malnutrition rates. - Post-acute phase: Stabilization with continued humanitarian response. - Rehabilitation phase: Efforts to restore normalcy and rebuild services. - Development phase: Long-term strategies to prevent future crises. - Chronic crisis phase: Prolonged food insecurity and conflict-related instability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify eight causes of nutrition emergencies. - Conflict and displacement. - Natural disasters (droughts, floods, earthquakes). - Economic crises. - Epidemics and disease outbreaks. - Poor governance and policy failures. - Disruptions in food supply chains. - Climate change impacts. - Lack of access to clean water and sanitation.

stem: Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of nutrition interventions in emergencies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline eight reasons for monitoring food and nutrition responses. - Ensuring program effectiveness and impact. - Identifying gaps in intervention coverage. - Preventing malnutrition-related mortality and morbidity. - Optimizing resource allocation. - Providing evidence for decision-making. - Strengthening accountability to donors and beneficiaries. - Detecting fraud and mismanagement. - Supporting advocacy efforts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss six challenges that face nutrition in emergencies. - Insecurity and conflict: Limits access to affected populations. - Limited funding and resources: Hinders comprehensive response. - Poor infrastructure: Difficulties in food distribution. - Lack of trained personnel: Affects intervention effectiveness. - Political and bureaucratic barriers: Delay response efforts. - Cultural and social constraints: Affect food acceptance and utilization. Abdul is 33 years old. His whole family loves soccer. They love to play and watch football. He is 6 feet tall and weighs 250 pounds. He played football in college but now that he has a job at a law firm working many hours, he plays once in a while on Saturdays. His family loves to eat potatoes and meat and they often barbecue ribs and hungers that are often washed down with several beers. During week days, he normally gets coffee and doughnuts delivered to his office for breakfast and goes to lunch with clients at various restaurants. Abdul knows that he has been gaining weight but stills feels pretty good. A few years ago, his cousin was diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Recently Abdul’s father was diagnosed with colorectal cancer too. He now routinely visits his nutritionist for dietary advice and nutrition assessment as advised by the family doctor.

stem: Give four reasons for fair dismissal from an employment contract. - - Gross misconduct - - Incapacity due to ill health - - Redundancy or retrenchment - - Breach of contract terms by employee SECTION B Question 11 Japheth is a licensed dietitian running a private nutrition consultancy in Nairobi. He offers personalized dietary plans, home visits, and corporate wellness programs. Concerned about possible legal claims from clients with allergic reactions, Japheth took out a professional liability insurance policy with a local insurer. Three months later, a client filed a claim, alleging that a recommended supplement caused severe side effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two classes of insurance relevant to Japheth’s case. - Professional indemnity insurance – covers claims arising from professional advice or services. - Public liability insurance – covers claims by third parties for bodily injury or property damage on the business premises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mention six steps in the claims procedure that Japheth should follow. - - Notify the insurer promptly of the claim. - - Complete and submit the official claim form. - - Provide detailed client medical records and incident report. - - Cooperate with the insurer’s investigation. - - Attend any required mediation or dispute‐resolution meetings. - - Accept the insurer’s settlement or decide to pursue legal action.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two principles of insurance demonstrated in this case. - Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) – both parties must disclose all material facts. - Indemnity – insurance restores the insured to the financial position before the loss.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain three importance of insurance for professionals in food and nutrition. - - Risk transfer – shifts financial liability for professional claims to the insurer. - - Legal compliance – meets regulatory or contractual requirements for practice. - - Business continuity – protects against large payouts that could threaten business viability. Question 12 NutriLife Wellness Centre is a private nutrition clinic that recently dismissed Kadzo, one of its employees. The company claims that Kadzo has gross misconduct and repeated absenteeism without proper cause. However, Kadzo claims she was never issued any prior warning or disciplinary notice, as required by her employment contract. She also argues that the termination was sudden and did not follow due process as per the employment agreement she signed. She has decided to sue NutriLife for unlawful dismissal and breach of contract.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss five essential elements of a valid employment contract. - - Offer and acceptance – clear terms offered by employer and accepted by employee. - - Consideration – mutual exchange of value, e.g., salary for services. - - Capacity – parties must have legal ability to enter contract. - - Legality of object – contract’s purpose must be lawful. - - Intention to create legal relations – parties intend legal enforceability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain five possible remedies available to Kadzo following breach of her employment contract. - - Reinstatement – return to former position. - - Compensation – payment for lost wages. - - Damages – financial award for losses from breach. - - Specific performance – court order to fulfill contractual duties. - - Injunction – prevent employer from further breach. Question 13 Samantha is a registered nutritionist who has worked in a government hospital for three years. She now wants to open her own nutrition clinic and offer private dietetics services. She is unsure of the legal requirements for obtaining a private practice license from the Kenya Nutritionists and Dieticians Institute (KNDI).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify five legal and professional requirements for obtaining a KNDI private practice license. - - Valid KNDI professional registration. - - Degree or diploma in Nutrition and Dietetics from a recognized institution. - - Professional indemnity insurance coverage. - - Clean criminal record/certificate of good conduct. - - Evidence of continuing professional development (CPD) credits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline seven steps of applying for a private practice license through the KNDI portal. - - Register an account on the KNDI portal. - - Complete the online application form. - - Upload certified copies of qualifications. - - Pay the application/licensing fee. - - Schedule and pass premises inspection if required. - - Submit proof of professional indemnity insurance. - - Download and print the license upon approval.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain four consequences of practicing without a valid KNDI private practice license. - - Fines and penalties as per Nutritionists and Dietitians Act. - - Closure of the unlicensed practice. - - Professional misconduct proceedings and deregistration. - - Loss of credibility and public trust. Question 14 Food safety and hygiene are essential in preventing foodborne illnesses, particularly in informal urban food establishments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain five responsibilities of public health officers in enforcing food safety regulations under the Public Health Act. - - Inspect food premises for hygiene and compliance. - - Issue improvement notices or closure orders for violations. - - Collect and analyze food/water samples for contaminants. - - Provide education and guidance to food handlers. - - Prosecute operators for public health offenses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain five ways in which the Foods and Drugs Act helps to protect the health of consumers. - - Regulates food additives and preservatives. - - Sets labeling and packaging standards. - - Controls import/export quality of foods and drugs. - - Prohibits sale of adulterated or contaminated products. - - Enables recall of unsafe products and penalties for violations.
